q: What two jobs does perfusion do?

opts.t: Bring oxygen and nutrients in; take waste out
opts.why: Perfusion pumps blood so cells get oxygen and sugar and waste leaves.

opts.t: Bring waste in; take oxygen and nutrients out
opts.why: That swaps the jobs. Perfusion delivers oxygen and nutrients and removes waste.

opts.t: Bring oxygen in; skip removing any waste
opts.why: Both jobs matter. Waste (CO₂, later lactic acid) has to leave too.

opts.t: Bring waste in; skip delivering any oxygen
opts.why: Cells need oxygen and nutrients in, not waste in.

q: For an EMT, shock is which of these?

opts.why: Shock = hypoperfusion = a circulatory / perfusion problem.
Hyper is too much flow. Shock is hypo: not enough perfusion.
Adequate perfusion is the healthy state, not shock.
Aerobic work is what cells do when perfusion is already good.

q: When perfusion is adequate, what is the main cell waste?

opts.why: Aerobic metabolism needs oxygen, makes lots of ATP, and wastes CO₂ that is easy to clear.
Lactic acid is the anaerobic waste when perfusion is already failing.
Aerobic cells use oxygen. The waste they make is carbon dioxide.
Glucose is fuel going in, not the aerobic waste product.

q: When perfusion is inadequate, what is the main cell waste?

opts.why: Anaerobic work makes less energy and lactic acid, which is hard to clear and adds acidosis.
CO₂ is the aerobic waste. Shock cells switch to lactic acid.
These cells are short on oxygen. Their waste is lactic acid.
Glucose is fuel. The anaerobic waste is lactic acid.

q: Without oxygen, how long do brain and heart last?

opts.why: Brain and heart injure and die in minutes. That is why time is critical.
Hours is the skin and gut clock, not brain and heart.
Brain and heart do not last days without oxygen.
The recap clock for brain and heart is minutes, not seconds.

q: Without oxygen, how long do skin and intestines last?

opts.why: Skin and gut last hours. They still get injured, just slower. Brain and heart come first.
Minutes is the brain and heart clock, not skin and gut.
The recap clock for skin and gut is hours, not days.
Seconds is too fast. Skin and gut last hours.

q: Heart rate up, harder squeeze, some vessels tight so heart and brain keep blood. What is this?

opts.why: Sympathetic epinephrine raises rate and squeeze and tightens some beds to protect heart and brain.
Those epi moves are compensation, not the late collapse.
This is a vessel-and-heart response, not the aerobic waste path.
This fires because perfusion is dropping, not because flow is too high.

q: Fast pulse, fast breathing, cool pale clammy skin, blood pressure still normal. What is this?

opts.why: Early compensation can hold the pressure. Do not wait for hypotension to name it.
Decompensated shock has a falling pressure and a much worse mental status.
Cool pale clammy skin and a fast pulse are not adequate perfusion.
Hyper is too much flow. These signs are early low perfusion.

q: Falling blood pressure, much worse mental status, very weak or absent wrist pulses, mottled very cool skin. What is this?

opts.why: When compensation fails you get hypotension, a worse mental status, and failing pulses and skin.
Compensated shock still holds a near-normal pressure.
These are late shock signs, not adequate perfusion.
Hyper is too much flow. This is late low perfusion.
Shock can exist before blood pressure drops. Read mental status, skin, and pulses first.
Waiting for hypotension means you missed compensated shock.

opts.t: Call it from heart rate only
opts.why: A fast pulse is one sign, not the whole perfusion check.

opts.t: Call it from cap refill only
opts.why: Cap refill can help. Name shock from perfusion signs, not one test.

q: Besides blood pressure, what do you check first for perfusion?

opts.why: Perfusion status first: mental status, skin signs, pulses. Blood pressure is a clue, not the whole story.

opts.t: Heart rate, cap refill, and SBP
opts.why: Heart rate and cap refill can help, but the recap’s first look is mental status, skin, and pulses.
Do not lead with the pressure number. Mental status, skin, and pulses come first.
Cap refill is extra. The recap’s first look is mental status, skin, and pulses.

q: Why keep a shock patient warm?

opts.why: Less energy means less heat, so they slide toward hypothermia in the lethal triad.
Shock cells are anaerobic. They make less heat, not extra heat.
Cold is a problem (hypothermia), not a treatment for lactic acid.
Keep them warm. Hypothermia is part of the lethal triad, not a clearance trick.
